title: Reductivity and maximality of a split torus persist near a fibre
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], and let $G\to S$ be a smooth affine group scheme of finite presentation [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. An $S$-group scheme has multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme], with $S$ in place of the field base. Write $\mathbf G_{m,S}=\operatorname{Spec}_S\mathcal O_S[t,t^{-1}]$ with multiplication of units, and $\mathbf G_{m,S}^0=1_S$. For $s\in|S|$, write $G_{\bar s}^0$ for the identity connected component of the fibre over an algebraic closure of $\kappa(s)$, with its open-subscheme structure; connectedness is [def-weil-connected-scheme]. A group over an algebraically closed field is reductive if it is smooth, connected, affine of finite type and has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup; unipotent means that geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful representation. A torus over that field is a group isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^d$ for some $d\geq0$, and maximal means maximal among such closed subgroups. Suppose $G_{\bar s}^0$ is reductive for a point $s\in|S|$. Then there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $s$ such that $G_{\bar u}^0$ is reductive for every geometric point $\bar u\to U$. Moreover, if $r\geq0$ and $j:\mathbf G_{m,S}^r\hookrightarrow G$ is a closed subgroup immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] whose geometric fibre $j_{\bar s}$ is a maximal torus of $G_{\bar s}^0$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $s$ such that $j_{\bar v}$ is a maximal torus of $G_{\bar v}^0$ for every geometric point $\bar v\to V$.

source.place: WANTED locally; Brian Conrad, Reductive group schemes (2014), Proposition 3.1.9(1),(2), printed pp.85-88 (split-torus instance of (2)); read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/luminysga3smf.pdf

proof.text: We may restrict the base to an affine neighborhood of $s$. Let $H$ be the open component locus of the identity section in $G$, given by [lem-sbc-smooth-section-component-open]. Its geometric fibres are $G_{\bar u}^0$: connected smooth field groups remain connected under field extension by [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products], and their identity components are open-and-closed subgroup schemes by [lem-sfb-finite-type-group-identity-subgroup]. The group diagrams restrict to this open because they restrict on every geometric fibre, so $H$ is an open subgroup, smooth by [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-restrict-open-subschemes]; we do not assert that $H$ is affine over $S$. Each $H_{\bar u}$ is affine of finite type, being an open-and-closed component of the affine finite-type fibre. The same component-locus construction will be used for other smooth affine groups below.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9 proof, printed pp.85-86; relative identity component as in Proposition 3.1.1

proof.text: First suppose a split torus $T=\mathbf G_{m,S}^r\hookrightarrow G$ is given and $T_{\bar s}$ is maximal in the reductive $H_{\bar s}$. Put $C=C_G(T)$, smooth affine and finitely presented by [lem-sfb-relative-torus-centralizer-normalizer]. On the special geometric fibre, $C_{\bar s}^0=C_{H_{\bar s}}(T_{\bar s})=T_{\bar s}$: connectedness of the torus centralizer in $H_{\bar s}$ is [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected], and its equality with $T_{\bar s}$ is [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer]. Thus $\dim C_{\bar s}=r$. By [lem-sfb-smooth-group-fibre-dimension], shrink around $s$ so that $\dim C_{\bar u}=r$ for every geometric fibre. Any torus in $H_{\bar u}$ properly containing $T_{\bar u}$ lies in $C_{\bar u}$, and has dimension greater than $r$ by the strict-dimension assertion of [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products], a contradiction. This proves the maximality assertion. Moreover $C_{H_{\bar u}}(T_{\bar u})$ is smooth connected by [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected], contains $T_{\bar u}$ and has dimension at most $r$, so the same strict-dimension assertion gives $C_{H_{\bar u}}(T_{\bar u})=T_{\bar u}$. This argument has not assumed reductivity away from $s$.

To prove the first assertion, choose a maximal torus $j_0:\mathbf G_{m,\Omega}^r\hookrightarrow H_{\bar s}$ by [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], where $\Omega=\overline{\kappa(s)}$. Compose with $H_{\bar s}\hookrightarrow G_{\bar s}$. Apply [lem-sfb-geometric-torus-fppf-lift] to obtain $p:S'\to S$, $s'$ over $s$ and a split closed torus $T\hookrightarrow G_{S'}$ extending $j_0$. Work on an affine neighborhood of $s'$ and apply the already proved step 2 there. For now rename this base $S$ and its point $s$; all geometric fibre centralizers $C_{H_{\bar u}}(T_{\bar u})$ equal $T_{\bar u}$. At the end we take the image of the final open neighborhood under the original flat finitely presented map $p$; the exact descent argument is step 10.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9 proof (1), printed p.86, first paragraph

proof.text: Write $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $M=\mathbf Z^r=X^*(T)$. By [lem-sfb-relative-torus-centralizer-normalizer], $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is finite locally free and base-change compatible. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-torus-bundle-weights] to its conjugation coaction. At $\bar s$, [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] gives weight zero of dimension $r$, a finite set $\Phi$ of nonzero weights of dimension one each, and $\mathbf Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. There are only finitely many summands on this affine base; shrink so that all their ranks are constant. Consequently on every geometric fibre the nonzero weights are exactly $\Phi$, with dimension one, and the zero weight has dimension $r$. Empty $\Phi$ is allowed.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9 proof (1), printed pp.86-87, weight-space paragraph

proof.text: For each $\alpha\in\Phi$, let $L_\alpha=M\cap\mathbf Q\alpha$ and put $K_\alpha=\operatorname{Spec}A[M/L_\alpha]\subseteq T$. Concretely divide the integer coordinates of $\alpha$ by their greatest common divisor to get a primitive vector $\beta$; elementary integer row operations put $\beta$ first in a basis of $M$. The quotient $M/L_\alpha$ is therefore free of rank $r-1$, and the displayed inclusion is, in these coordinates, the subtorus with first coordinate $1$. A character $m$ restricts trivially precisely when $m\in L_\alpha$. Thus [lem-sfb-relative-torus-bundle-weights] identifies the invariant tangent bundle with the sum of the zero, $\alpha$ and $-\alpha$ summands, of total rank $r+2$. This uses the reducedness condition from step 4 and remains valid when $\alpha$ is not primitive or the residue characteristic divides its coordinates.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9 proof (1), printed p.87, construction of T_alpha and invariant-weight calculation

proof.text: Put $J_\alpha=C_G(K_\alpha)$, smooth affine finitely presented with base-change compatible Lie algebra by [lem-sfb-relative-torus-centralizer-normalizer]. On a geometric fibre let $H_{\alpha,\bar u}=C_{H_{\bar u}}(K_{\alpha,\bar u})$. It is smooth connected by [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected], and equals $(J_{\alpha,\bar u})^0$: its points belong to $H_{\bar u}$, while the identity component of $J_{\alpha,\bar u}$ lies in the identity component of $G_{\bar u}$. Its Lie dimension is $r+2$ by step 5 and the centralizer Lie formula, so its dimension is $r+2$ by [lem-sfb-group-tangent-dimension-smoothness]. It contains the central torus $K_{\alpha,\bar u}$ of dimension $r-1$, and $T_{\bar u}$ is maximal in it by step 2. Its special fibre is reductive by [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-fixed-subgroup] applied in $H_{\bar s}$.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9 proof (1), printed p.87, reduction to corank-one centralizers

proof.text: Fix $\alpha\in\Phi$. Apply [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] in the original special reductive group $H_{\bar s}$. It gives a normalizer element $n_\alpha\in H_{\alpha,\bar s}(\Omega)$ whose induced automorphism $\sigma_\alpha$ of $T_{\bar s}$ sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-torus-centralizer-normalizer] to $T\subseteq J_\alpha$. Inside its smooth normalizer take the open-and-closed locus with action matrix $\sigma_\alpha$, and intersect with the relative identity-component open of $J_\alpha$ from [lem-sbc-smooth-section-component-open]. Call this open scheme $W_\alpha$. It is smooth over the base, and its image contains $s$ because it contains $n_\alpha$ on that geometric fibre. By [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-restrict-open-subschemes] it is smooth, hence flat and locally of finite presentation by [lem-pc-smooth-flat]; [lem-weil-pbc-flat-lfp-open] makes its image open. Replace the base by the intersection of these finitely many open images. For every geometric point of this base, $W_\alpha$ has a point after some extension to an algebraically closed field. Such a point normalizes $T$, lies in the identity component of $J_\alpha$, and does not centralize $T$, since $\alpha\ne-\alpha$ in the free lattice $M$.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9 proof (1), printed p.88, lifting the nontrivial Weyl element; use the open image of its normalizer action locus

proof.text: Every $H_{\alpha,\bar u}$ is nonsolvable. Otherwise it remains smooth connected and solvable after the algebraically closed extension in step 7, by [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products]. Apply [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus] there to obtain a normal unipotent subgroup with torus quotient $q:H_\alpha\to D$. Since $T$ is maximal, [lem-sfb-solvable-torus-complements] says $q|_T$ is an isomorphism. For the normalizer element $n$ of step 7, commutativity of $D$ gives $q(ntn^{-1})=q(t)$ on every algebra. Injectivity of $q|_T$ then gives $ntn^{-1}=t$ on every algebra, contradicting its action matrix. This proves nonsolvability on the original geometric fibre without assuming that the chosen normalizer point was already rational over its field.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9 proof (1), printed p.88, nonsolvability of the corank-one centralizers

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-nonsolvable-central-torus-corank-three], each $H_{\alpha,\bar u}$ is reductive: it is smooth connected affine, nonsolvable by step 8, contains the central torus $K_{\alpha,\bar u}$ and has $\dim H_{\alpha,\bar u}=r+2=(r-1)+3$. For every geometric fibre $H_{\bar u}$, the torus $T_{\bar u}$ is maximal and self-centralizing by step 2, and its nonzero weights are exactly $\Phi$ by step 4. Apply [lem-sfb-corank-one-centralizer-reductivity-test] to obtain reductivity of $H_{\bar u}$. If $\Phi$ is empty there were no $K_\alpha$ or normalizer-image restrictions, and the same criterion applies with its empty family. Thus the argument includes tori, trivial neutral fibres and rank zero.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9 proof (1), printed pp.87-88, Lemma 3.1.10 and final dimension argument

proof.text: Return to the base change $p:S'\to S$ of step 3, and let $O\subseteq S'$ be the final open neighborhood of $s'$ just obtained. Set $U=p(O)$; it is open and contains the original $s$ by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-lfp-open]. Given a geometric point $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to U$, the base change $O_\Omega$ is nonempty and quasi-finite of finite type over $\Omega$. Choose an affine open in it and a maximal ideal of its nonzero coordinate ring. That point has a finite residue extension of $\Omega$ by quasi-finiteness, so its residue field is $\Omega$, since $\Omega$ is algebraically closed. It gives a lift $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to O$. The geometric fibre of $G_O$ at this lift is precisely $G_\Omega$, with the same identity component. Step 9 proves its reductivity. Hence $U$ proves the first assertion. Step 2, applied directly to the torus specified in the question over the original base, gives the required $V$ for the second assertion.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9 proof (1), printed p.86, fppf-local reduction and descent to its open image

Small cases checked: r=0, Phi empty, non-primitive alpha, characteristic p.
